subject: Antarctic doctor
title: What If You Had to Remove Your Own Appendix? In 1961 a Doctor Did

scenes.text: What if the only doctor on an Antarctic base needed surgery? In 1961, he operated on himself.
April 29, 1961. At a Soviet station in Antarctica, the doctor, 27-year-old Leonid Rogozov, recognises the signs of appendicitis. In himself.
Blizzards rule out any flight. He is one of 12 men, and the only one who can operate.
The next night he numbs the area with local anaesthetic, half sitting up. Two crewmates assist, one holding a mirror.
He works mostly by touch, without gloves. After half an hour he's dizzy, resting about twenty seconds every few minutes.
One hour and 45 minutes later, it's done. The appendix was about a day from bursting. Two weeks on he was back at work, as the station's doctor.

description:
What if you were the only doctor for hundreds of kilometres and you needed surgery? On the night of 30 April 1961, Leonid Rogozov, 27, the only doctor among 12 men at the Soviet Novolazarevskaya station in Antarctica, removed his own appendix under local anaesthetic.
Blizzards made evacuation impossible. He worked mostly by touch for 1 hour 45 minutes, resting every few minutes; the stitches came out after a week and he was back on duty in about two.
This is history, not advice. What should we run through next?
thumbnail_text: WHAT IF YOU WERE THE ONLY DOCTOR?
first_comment: The nearest other station was roughly 1,000 kilometres away. Could you have kept your hands steady?
